source: Langley (1977) BACON: A production system that discovers empirical laws
finding: First BACON. A production system (OPS) in an artificial 2-D world. Regularity detectors fire on data in working memory. A constant leads to a generalisation. A steady rise or fall over time leads to a new attribute built from the change (acceleration from velocity). One value up while another goes down leads to a new product attribute. Detection and term construction steer new data collection.
numbers: Two techniques only: detect regularities, construct new terms. Data are attribute-object-time-value 4-tuples. Four-page paper with no counts of laws.
quote: once an hypothesis is formed, it is never rejected
limits: Author lists three limits: no conditional laws; built-in knowledge that time and objects are the dimensions to generalise over; cannot handle noise. Task world is artificial.
agent_relevance: The loop is: look for a constant or trend in what is computed, then define a new quantity and look again. This is a counted, code-run step, not a judged one, which fits G2 and G3.

source: Langley (1979) Rediscovering physics with BACON.3
finding: BACON.3 rediscovered five laws from generated data with one small set of heuristics: ideal gas law, Kepler's third law, Coulomb's law, Ohm's law, Galileo's laws (pendulum and constant acceleration). Its key idea is levels of description: a regularity at one level creates a higher level, and defined terms are treated like observed ones.
numbers: 86 OPS2 productions in 7 sets (17 gather data, 16 note regularities with constancy and trend detectors, 3 for term values, 22 for decomposing and checking new terms equal old ones, 3 to collapse descriptions with identical conditions, 8 for irrelevant terms). Ideal gas path: pV constant per (n,T), then pV/T linear in T with slope 8.32, then pV/nT = 8.32.
limits: Data were synthetic and clean; noise handled only by making LISP equal ignore small differences. Laws came out as products and ratios, so addition-type laws are out of reach. The PDF text is OCR-damaged but the logic is clear.
agent_relevance: Shows a recursive step: treat the output of a check as new data and apply the same check again. Our states could reuse one operator at rising levels instead of adding new operators (section 4b).

source: Langley (1979) Rediscovering physics with BACON.3 (complexity table)
finding: Cost differed a lot by law. Ohm's law took about four times the productions of the others. More terms related meant more levels and many rejected terms.
numbers: Productions fired: gas 1203, Kepler 1119, Coulomb 1297, Galileo 1150, Ohm 4593. Defined terms: 8, 17, 18, 9, 31. Redundant terms: 2, 1, 12, 7, 84. Levels: 4, 3, 4, 3, 5. Descriptions: 27, 18, 27, 23, 54.
limits: One run per law, no variance. Complexity is in production counts of this implementation only. OCR on the redundant-terms row is imperfect.
agent_relevance: A search over defined terms explodes without a redundancy check (84 redundant terms for Ohm). Our agent needs a code-side duplicate check on candidate hypotheses, not a model opinion.

source: Langley (1979) Rediscovering physics with BACON.3 (order effects and heuristic use)
finding: The final law did not depend on data order, but the cost did. Varying irrelevant variables (weight, angle for the pendulum) first found them irrelevant at once. Varying them last reached identical laws with more computation. Ideal gas with moles varied first took a different path (V/n, V/nT, pV/nT) to the same law.
numbers: Heuristic use table: collapsing descriptions used in all 5 tasks; ignoring differences in 4 of 5; irrelevant-variable rule in 1 (Galileo); different-experiments rule in 2.
limits: Author admits the irrelevant-variable result is misleading because irrelevant variables could be added to each task. Tasks were chosen by the author.
agent_relevance: Order robustness is testable: run the same data in shuffled order and demand the same final answer. A cheap check for G3 and G4.

source: Falkenhainer and Michalski (1986) Integrating quantitative and qualitative discovery: the ABACUS system
finding: ABACUS formulates equations over data subsets and also learns logic-style conditions saying when each equation holds (by joining with AQ11). It adds units analysis, proportionality-graph search and suspension search to narrow the search. It names BACON's weakness: the user must say which variables are dependent, and BACON.6 needs the law form supplied.
numbers: Cost in CPU seconds on a Sun workstation: ideal gas 15 events, 1 class, 3 nodes, 3 s total; momentum 22 events, 3 classes, 68 s; Coulomb 36 events, 5 classes, 32 nodes, 74 s; Stokes law 72 events, 6 classes, 49 s; kinetic energy 12 events, 2 classes, 987 nodes, 855 s; chemistry 30 events, 4 classes, 31 s.
quote: much of this power is achieved by requiring the user to provide a form of the answer
limits: Sums and differences are much harder than products and ratios. Noise: with 0.2 percent noise answers were correct, with 2 percent worse; the authors say real data would rule out 0.2 percent. Examples are small.
agent_relevance: Two laws for two subsets of data, each with a stated condition. Matches our need that a revision keeps its scope condition and does not overwrite a law that holds elsewhere.

source: Falkenhainer and Michalski (1986) ABACUS (BACON history and dimensional analysis)
finding: A rival group's account of BACON. BACON began in 1978; BACON.4 adds intrinsic properties and common divisors; BACON.5 adds symmetry; BACON.6 needs a given law form but handles trig and algebraic laws. Another line, Kokar's COPER and El-Shafei's HOTEP, uses dimensional analysis, which needs the relevant variables known first.
numbers: BACON.1 to BACON.6 across 1978-1986.
limits: Competitor's account of BACON; not checked against the Langley et al. 1987 book (not opened).
agent_relevance: Knowing units prunes the hypothesis space. A schema step could demand unit or scale consistency in code before any fit is tried.

source: Zytkow and Simon (1986) A theory of historical discovery: the construction of componential models
finding: STAHL rebuilds 18th-century componential chemistry. It takes reactions in the order they were published, infers components, then repairs conflicts. It reproduces the century-long phlogiston theory and also Black's models of mild alkali and Lavoisier's oxygen theory with the same rules.
numbers: Input is an ordered list of reactions with no fixed length limit. Example inference: charcoal burning means charcoal = phlogiston + ash. Heuristics for synthesis, decomposition, and error recovery from inconsistent models.
quote: it does not demonstrate that this path was taken historically
limits: Authors list limits: cannot generalise (oxygen + metal gives oxide + caloric), cannot use properties of substances, does not design experiments, and cannot choose between phlogiston and oxygen theory.
agent_relevance: Incremental feeding in historical order is a strong test because later inputs depend on the system's own earlier output. We can test our schema the same way on a case series.

source: Zytkow and Simon (1986) A theory of historical discovery (test design)
finding: States the validity problem of rediscovery work. One rediscovery (AM, BACON) only shows one possible path. A stronger test reproduces a sequence, including errors that experts held for a long time, with data fed piecemeal in historical order.
numbers: Criteria: conclusions accepted for a long time by several leading scientists are fair confirmatory tests; errors typical of the epoch are diagnostic.
limits: Not a quantified test. No human protocol comparison in this paper.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition on any claim that our step reproduces discovery X: the data must not be picked after the fact, and wrong turns must be reproduced too.

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: a physics-inspired method for symbolic regression
finding: Symbolic regression using dimensional analysis, polynomial fit, symmetry, separability, and a neural net to find structure. All 100 Feynman-Lectures equations were solved, against 71 for the best earlier public software per the abstract. Eureqa (the descendant of Schmidt and Lipson 2009) got 68 percent in the paper's own comparison.
numbers: Feynman set: AI Feynman 100 percent, Eureqa 68 percent. Bonus set of 20 harder equations: AI Feynman 90 percent, Eureqa 15 percent. On arbitrary mystery functions from an earlier paper: AI Feynman 66.7 percent, Eureqa 48.9 percent.
limits: The abstract says 71 and the key-findings text says 68 for the earlier software; setups differ. The Feynman equations are famous, so a text-trained model may have seen them. Performance drops on arbitrary compositions that lack symmetry or separability.
agent_relevance: The gain came from splitting the problem by structure found with checks (symmetry, separability), not from a bigger search. Same shape as our decompose-then-solve states.

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman (boundary conditions)
finding: Most of the 100 equations were still solved with only about 10^2 data points or percent-level noise. Performance on arbitrary equations unlikely to occur in physics is lower because the neural net part exploits symmetries that real physics has.
numbers: 66.7 versus 48.9 percent on non-physical equations; 100 versus 68 percent on physical ones.
limits: Success was defined as exact recovery within tolerance thresholds that were not tuned per equation.
agent_relevance: Methods that win by using the structure of real laws may fail on made-up tasks, and the reverse. Test a schema step on both real and synthetic problems.

source: Udrescu, Tan, Feng, Neto, Wu, Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman 2.0: Pareto-optimal symbolic regression exploiting graph modularity
finding: Keeps a Pareto frontier of formulas by accuracy against description length, merges frontiers recursively, and finds generalised modularity from gradients of a neural net. Also works on probability distributions from samples (normalising flows plus hypothesis tests).
numbers: Solves 73 of 100 baseline Feynman problems at noise 10^-1 (r = -1), typically 1 to 3 orders of magnitude more noise-robust than the previous version. 80 percent of ten sampled distributions were solved.
limits: Noise reduces apparent graph modularity, so modular structure can be missed. Robustness claim is relative to AI Feynman 1.0.
agent_relevance: Accuracy against simplicity as a code-computed trade-off (description length) is a selection rule that needs no model judge (G5).

source: Shojaee, Meidani, Gupta, Farimani, Reddy (2025) LLM-SR: scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs
finding: An LLM proposes equation skeletons as Python programs with free parameters. A code optimiser (BFGS or Adam) fits the parameters. Scored programs go in an experience buffer shown back to the LLM. It beat classical and neural symbolic regression on four tasks designed to avoid recitation (two custom nonlinear oscillators, E. coli growth, aluminium stress-strain).
numbers: About 2.5K iterations, 4 skeletons per prompt, temperature 0.8, k=2 in-context examples. Baselines ran over 2M iterations. E. coli out-of-domain NMSE about 0.0037 for LLM-SR; other methods above 1. Backbones GPT-3.5 and Mixtral. Baselines GPlearn, PySR, DSR, uDSR, NeSymReS, E2E.
limits: Four tasks only, on the authors' own benchmark. The table in the PDF text is scrambled so per-cell NMSE was not copied. Some LLM-SR cells are worse than PySR in-domain; the out-of-domain numbers carry the claim.
agent_relevance: A generate-fit-score-feedback loop with the LLM as proposer and code as judge matches our schema roles (section 1).

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR ablation
finding: Each component mattered on the Oscillation 2 problem with GPT-3.5. Removing the natural-language problem description hurt a lot; removing program form hurt less; removing the iterative refine loop and removing the skeleton plus separate optimiser both hurt much.
numbers: No iterative refinement: NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain and 1.81e-1 OOD. No skeleton plus optimiser: 3.78e-1 in-domain and 3.75e-1 OOD. numpy+BFGS slightly better than torch+Adam.
limits: One problem, one backbone, no repeated-seed variance in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Support for: do not let the model write numbers; let it write structure and let code fit the numbers. Also for the loop with real feedback (G2).

source: Shojaee, Nguyen, Meidani, Farimani, Doan, Reddy (2025) LLM-SRBench
finding: Benchmark built to defeat memorisation. LSR-Transform rewrites Feynman equations into less common forms by changing which variable is the output. LSR-Synth makes new synthetic problems in four fields. The best system found only about 31 percent of equations.
numbers: 239 problems: 111 LSR-Transform plus 128 LSR-Synth (chemistry, biology, physics, material science). Best symbolic accuracy 31.5 percent on LSR-Transform and 28.1 percent on LSR-Synth.
limits: Symbolic accuracy is judged by GPT-4o comparing expressions. Transformations keep the physics, so some memorised knowledge may still help.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent evidence that rediscovery of famous laws overstates skill. For our tests use transformed or synthetic cases, not the classic law as published.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench (memorisation test and method grid)
finding: Plain sampling from Llama-3.1-8B on 100 original Feynman problems shows sharp early drops in error and low symbolic error, read as memorisation. The transformed set shows gradual, higher error. At equal expression size the transformed problems stayed harder, so it is not just complexity.
numbers: Symbolic accuracy percent on LSR-Transform: direct prompt Llama-3.1-8B 3.61, GPT-3.5 2.10, GPT-4o-mini 7.21; LaSR GPT-3.5 12.61; LLM-SR Llama-3.1-8B 30.63, GPT-3.5 10.81, GPT-4o-mini 31.53.
limits: Table cells in the PDF text are partly scrambled; only cleanly readable cells are quoted. Backbones are small by 2026 standards.
agent_relevance: A data-blind prompt gets 2 to 7 percent; adding a fit-and-feedback loop gets about 31 percent for the best backbones. The loop adds much of the gain, not the model alone.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench (out-of-domain link)
finding: Symbolic accuracy correlates strongly and positively with out-of-domain numeric precision and negatively with out-of-domain error. Out-of-domain error is higher than in-domain for all methods. Good numeric fit can sit beside low symbolic accuracy.
numbers: LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini on the material-science column: Acc0.1 88.28 percent but symbolic accuracy 20.24 percent.
limits: One cell of a scrambled table; read as an example, not a summary.
agent_relevance: Matches G3: passing the given numbers does not prove the law. Require a held-out or extrapolation check.

source: Grayeli, Sehgal, Costilla-Reyes, Cranmer, Chaudhuri (2024) Symbolic regression with a learned concept library (LaSR)
finding: LaSR adds a library of abstract text concepts, induced by an LLM from the best hypotheses, to the PySR genetic search. The LLM is called with small probability p. It solved more of the 100 Feynman equations than all baselines.
numbers: Exact solves out of 100: GPlearn 20, AFP 24, AFP-FE 26, DSR 23, uDSR 40, AI Feynman 38, PySR 59, LaSR 72. With Llama3-8B: p=1 percent 67, p=5 percent 69, p=10 percent 71. LaSR with GPT-3.5 at p=1 percent: 72.
limits: Feynman equations are well known and may be in LLM training data (see LLM-SRBench). On LSR-Transform LaSR scored only about 6 to 13 percent symbolic accuracy in that benchmark's runs.
agent_relevance: Calling the LLM on 1 to 10 percent of steps already beats the search without it. The LLM is a sparse helper here, not the loop's driver.

source: Xia, Sun, Liu (2026) SR-Scientist: scientific equation discovery with agentic AI
finding: The LLM is an agent with code tools: analyse data, write the equation as code, submit for scoring, revise on feedback over a long horizon with an experience buffer. It beat baselines on four science fields by 6 to 35 points absolute. A reinforcement-learning stage lifted a 30B model.
numbers: Best: GPT-OSS-120B backbone, Acc0.01 63.57 and Acc0.001 49.35 on LSR-Synth. Ablation with GPT backbone: no data-analysis tool 35.66 and 16.28; no experience buffer 57.36 and 41.86; no top-k 58.14 and 41.86. About 1000 LLM calls per problem. Runs repeated three times and averaged.
limits: LSR-Synth only. Two authors checked for data contamination. Compute cost is high.
agent_relevance: The largest ablation effect came from letting the model compute statistics with a tool, the code side of the loop (G2, G5). Memory of past tries mattered less with the GPT backbone.

source: Xia, Sun, Liu (2026) SR-Scientist (backbone differences)
finding: Ablations differ by backbone. With Qwen3-Coder-480B removing the buffer cost about 13 points of Acc0.01 and removing top-k about 23; with GLM-4.5-Air the data tool mattered little (48.32 to 46.51).
numbers: Qwen: full 49.09, no tool 41.08, no buffer 35.66, no top-k 26.36 (Acc0.01). GLM: full 48.32, no tool 46.51, no buffer 37.21, no top-k 41.96.
limits: Three repeats averaged; no confidence intervals in the table.
agent_relevance: Which scaffold part matters depends on the model. Ablate per backbone before keeping an element (G7).

source: Ma et al. (2024) LLM and simulation as bilevel optimizers: Scientific Generative Agent (SGA)
finding: Bilevel loop: the LLM proposes discrete parts (equation form, molecule), differentiable simulation fits the continuous parameters and gives feedback. Tested on 4 constitutive-law tasks and 4 molecule-design tasks. An imaginary constitutive law was built to keep the LLM from reciting.
numbers: 8 tasks in total. Compared with DSO, Operon and others on a symbolic constitutive task.
limits: Needs a specific simulator. Numbers in the text were not clean enough to quote.
agent_relevance: The imaginary-law trick is a cheap contamination control we can reuse (G8).

source: Wang, Wang, Li, Zhang, Cheng (2025) DrSR: dual reasoning from data and experience
finding: Adds a data-analysis step (monotonicity, nonlinearity, correlation) and a reflection step over positive, negative and error outcomes to an LLM-SR style loop. It claims better valid-equation rate, accuracy and efficiency than LLM-SR.
numbers: Accuracy above 90 percent on several benchmarks with Mixtral and LLaMA backbones. Idea library draws from the last 50 percent of entries per category.
limits: Authors' own runs; gains vary by dataset.
agent_relevance: Negative and error examples kept next to good ones: a cheap memory design for revision from real output (G2).

source: MOOSE-Chem authors (2025) LLMs for rediscovering unseen chemistry scientific hypotheses
finding: Rediscovery without data: split discovery into retrieve inspiration, compose hypothesis, rank. Benchmark of 51 chemistry papers published after January 2024, annotated by PhD chemists, tested with models whose training ended before 2024, so no leakage.
numbers: Hit ratio of ground-truth inspirations kept after screening a 300-paper corpus (top 4 percent kept): GPT-4o 83.7, Llama-3.1-70B 83.0, Llama-3.1-405B 78.7, Llama-3.1-8B 43.5. At top 20 percent: 96.7, 95.1, 95.7, 71.6.
limits: Match of generated hypotheses is mostly graded by GPT-4o. Ranking by the model's own score tracks match weakly (average rank ratio 0.411 to 0.521 across match levels).
agent_relevance: Model self-ranking of ideas is weak, which backs G8. Retrieval of the right inspiration is strong, so a retrieve-then-combine step is worth testing.

source: Cranmer et al. (2020) Discovering symbolic models from deep learning with inductive biases
finding: Train a graph network with sparse messages, then fit symbolic regression to its parts. It recovered known force laws and Hamiltonians and found a new formula for dark-matter halo overdensity from simulation. The symbolic formula generalised out of distribution better than the network.
numbers: Tested forces: 1/r, 1/r^2, charged, damped springs, discontinuous. Cosmology example from a dark-matter simulation.
limits: The new formula is judged by fit and generalisation, not an independent derivation. Needs sparse latent structure.
agent_relevance: Two-stage idea: learn a model, then compress it into a law and test the law out of distribution (G3).

source: Cranmer (2023) PySR and SymbolicRegression.jl
finding: Open-source multi-population evolutionary symbolic regression, the base for LaSR. Reviewed against AI Feynman and SRBench.
numbers: LaSR reports PySR at 59 of 100 Feynman equations.
limits: I read only the design and benchmark parts.
agent_relevance: A strong cheap non-LLM baseline; any LLM discovery claim should be set against it at equal compute (G7).

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: Computational Explorations of the Creative Processes
finding: The founding book: BACON.1 to BACON.6, GLAUBER (qualitative laws), STAHL (componential models), DALTON (atomic theory) and others, each run on a historical episode. Central claim: discovery is heuristic search in problem spaces and needs no special faculty.
numbers: Not opened (borrow-only copy). Counts above come from the ABACUS and Zytkow-Simon papers.
limits: Most programs got data already cleaned and variables already chosen, a standing criticism.
agent_relevance: Frames each schema state as a heuristic search step with named, countable operators.

source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Dual space search during scientific reasoning
finding: Adults programmed a toy robot (the Big Trak) and had to find what a hidden repeat key did. Search ran in two linked spaces: hypotheses and experiments. Subjects differed in style, theorists versus experimenters.
numbers: Not opened (Wiley blocked); no sample size or percentages recorded from memory.
limits: Single task; adult college students.
agent_relevance: Our states can be read as moves in a hypothesis space and an experiment space; test which space a stall sits in.

source: Klahr and Simon (1999) Studies of scientific discovery: complementary approaches and convergent findings
finding: Review joining computational rediscovery with human lab studies of discovery. Claims the two lines agree: discovery uses search in problem spaces, weak methods and experiment space.
numbers: Not opened (paywalled); no numbers recorded.
limits: A review by the program's own founders.
agent_relevance: The bridge to human data; pair with Klahr-Dunbar numbers once read.

source: Schmidt and Lipson (2009) Distilling free-form natural laws from experimental data
finding: Eureqa: genetic programming searches equations and favours ones that predict derivatives of the data, a test that does not depend on a fixed equation form. It found conservation laws and equations for motion systems such as a double pendulum from raw data.
numbers: Not opened (paywalled). Eureqa's later benchmark score comes from AI Feynman: 68 percent of 100 Feynman equations.
limits: Unopened; details from memory only.
agent_relevance: A check built on derivatives, not on fit to the given points, is a model for G3.
